content: Kawasaki disease (KD) is a condition that can lead to damage in the heart and blood vessels, primarily affecting children under the age of 5. Boys are more frequently affected than girls. The exact cause of KD remains unknown. In the United States, the incidence of KD is estimated to range from 9 to 20 cases per 100,000 children under 5 years old. In 2019, over 5,000 children under the age of 18 were hospitalized with KD in the U.S., with 3,693 of these cases occurring in children under 5 years old. This corresponds to a hospitalization rate of 18.9 per 100,000 children in this age group. Children with KD typically present with a fever lasting at least 5 days. Additional symptoms may include a rash, redness and swelling of the hands and feet, redness of the whites of the eyes, swollen lymph nodes in the neck, and irritation or inflammation of the mouth, lips, and throat. Not all children will exhibit all of these symptoms. KD can lead to severe complications, such as swelling in the coronary arteries and other blood vessels. This can impair the heart's ability to pump blood effectively and, in severe cases, may result in coronary artery dilation or aneurysms. For healthcare professionals, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) defines a case of KD as a patient with a fever lasting 5 or more days (or until intravenous immunoglobulin is administered, if given before the fifth day of fever) and at least 4 of the following 5 clinical signs: rash, swelling and redness of the hands and feet, cervical lymphadenopathy (lymph nodes in the neck measuring at least 1.5 cm in diameter), bilateral conjunctival injection (redness in both eyes), and changes in the oral mucosa (such as redness, cracking, or inflammation of the lips and mouth). Patients who do not meet this case definition but have fever and coronary artery abnormalities are classified as having atypical or incomplete KD. Healthcare professionals can report cases using the CDC's standardized KD case report form. Treatment for KD is available and must be administered in a hospital setting. The standard treatment involves intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and aspirin, which help reduce the severity of symptoms and lower the risk of serious complications. Additional treatments may be recommended by healthcare providers based on the individual case. With appropriate treatment, most children recover fully. There have also been reports of conditions resembling Kawasaki disease following infection with SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19. This condition is referred to as multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C).
